method: Sixth clause checked via CourtListener this session (egress to statute hosts still blocked, re-probed the same day, unchanged). The clause's claim ('no expectation of privacy in data stored on or transmitted through Company systems') is a common handbook assertion with a well-developed, genuinely mixed body of case law behind it -- not a single clean rule -- so two opinions representing the two poles of that case law were read rather than the first one found.
queries: Stengart v. Loving Care Agency personal email company computer expectation of privacy (CourtListener, N.J. 2010)
"reasonable expectation of privacy" -- read within the Stengart opinion
Smyth v. Pillsbury Co. company e-mail no reasonable expectation of privacy (CourtListener, E.D. Pa. 1996, cited within Stengart)

assertions.text: employees have no reasonable expectation of privacy in communications made over the Company's own email system
assertions.note: Smyth v. Pillsbury Co., 914 F.Supp. 97, 100-01 (E.D. Pa. 1996), quoted below -- the case Stengart itself cites as the leading authority for this proposition. Directly on point and not narrowed by anything read in this check.

assertions.text: employees have no expectation of privacy in ANY data stored on or transmitted through Company systems, stated without qualification
assertions.note: Stengart v. Loving Care Agency, Inc., 990 A.2d 650 (N.J. 2010), quoted below -- a personal, password-protected webmail account accessed on a company-owned laptop retained a reasonable expectation of privacy despite a company policy purporting to eliminate one, particularly because the messages were attorney-client communications. The court held the question 'must be addressed on a case-by-case basis' (quoting O'Connor v. Ortega, 480 U.S. 709, 718 (1987)), not resolved categorically by an employer policy statement. The clause's own 'should have no expectation of privacy' sentence carries no such qualification.

gaps: The clause's 'no expectation of privacy... on Company systems' is accurate for the ordinary case Smyth addresses (an employee's ordinary use of the company's own email/systems) but is stated as though monitoring is therefore unconstrained. Stengart's own fact pattern is exactly the scenario this clause's last sentence gestures at without addressing -- an employee using a personal, password-protected account (there, webmail; the clause separately tells employees not to store confidential information in personal accounts, which implies personal accounts are in scope of employee behavior but not of what the Company may do with them) accessed through a company device. Personal accounts accessed on Company hardware are not squarely 'data stored on or transmitted through Company systems,' and the clause does not say whether the Company claims any monitoring right over them.

Privileged communications (attorney-client, in Stengart's case) get separate, stronger protection than ordinary personal communications under the case law read here. The clause draws no distinction for privileged content at all.

Courts described in Stengart's own survey (not independently read here, only as characterized by Stengart itself) draw a further distinction between accessing personal webmail through a browser versus routing personal messages through the company's own email address -- the latter looking more like Smyth even when the content is personal. The clause does not address this distinction because it does not address personal accounts at all.

The clause's own advance-written-notice requirement ('may require advance written notice') for state-law monitoring rules was not itself checked against any specific state's statute -- every host that would carry state notice-of-monitoring statutes was blocked.

judicialQuotations.case: Smyth v. Pillsbury Co. (E.D. Pa. 1996) 914 F.Supp. 97
judicialQuotations.quote: we do not find a reasonable expectation of privacy in e-mail communications voluntarily made by an employee to his supervisor over the company e-mail system notwithstanding any assurances that such communications would not be intercepted by management. Once plaintiff communicated the alleged unprofessional comments to a second person (his supervisor) over an email system which was apparently utilized by the entire company, any reasonable expectation of privacy was lost.

judicialQuotations.case: Stengart v. Loving Care Agency, Inc. (N.J. 2010) 990 A.2d 650
judicialQuotations.quote: we find that Stengart had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the e-mails she exchanged with her attorney on Loving Care's laptop. Stengart plainly took steps to protect the privacy of those e-mails and shield them from her employer. She used a personal, password-protected e-mail account instead of her company e-mail address and did not save the account's password on her computer.

judicialQuotations.case: Stengart v. Loving Care Agency, Inc. (N.J. 2010) 990 A.2d 650
judicialQuotations.quote: whether an employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy in her particular work setting 'must be addressed on a case-by-case basis.'
